comment_text.value:
I'm having a real existential crisis over the internet and technology. On the one hand, LLMs are allowing me to build and explore and learn more than I have ever been able to do before. I'm a kid in a candy store.

On the other hand, I really hate what social media has become. I'm addicted to Reddit and I hate it. I hate the toxicity of the community. I hate the rage algorithms. I hate the brain rot content. The rest of the internet is no better. Websites have become marketing funnels. Dark patterns designed to squeeze every second of attention and every cent out of users.

Ultimately I feel I have all the tools required to just walk away from the "bad" parts of the internet, but I can't. I liken this to people who cannot lose weight. It's simple to just eat less, but it's not easy. I can't help but feel that we've structured society around encouraging us (in extremely well-researched and optimised ways) to be as unhealthy as possible in every way. Physically, mentally, spiritually, socially, economically.

I have become at least somewhat sympathetic towards paternalistic governing structures around the world like China. I am painfully aware of all of the atrocious human rights abuses and lack of freedoms, but when they saw children becoming addicted to social media and committing suicide at much higher rates, they acted and either banned kids, or severely limited access. When they saw TikTok turn children's brains into mush, they mandated that the content be educational and aspirational.

I guess what I'm saying is: I don't think human psyches have evolved to deal with this level of psychological manipulation. Professional testing shows my IQ to be well above average, and I'm failing. The average person doesn't stand a chance. I think we need much tougher regulations on this stuff, but I don't trust any of our politicians to do it competently or with our best interests in mind.

While I agree with the majority of the text, I really don't understand why the amateurish efforts of so many are taken so seriously, to the point where people actually obsess over them. The marketing of these outputs by individuals or organizations with no prior connection to the industry (especially on platforms like YouTube, Reddit, HackerNews, etc.) is driven solely by self-interest. These ideas only excite the laypeople and the naive. For a professional or anyone who actually knows how things work, these are—as the name implies—just tools for now, not the be-all and end-all.

comment_text.value:
For those who've said that advertising has led them to previously unknown / unrealised products or opportunities....

I've spent much time over the past few years trying to research some major purchases: household appliances, personal electronics, furniture, health-care items, data and communications services.

I'm actively looking for valid information. And despite the present insanely-advanced information ecosystem we have, it's an utter shitshow.

Advertising is all but worthless. There was a time when advertising actually contained voluntarily-supplied (as opposed to regulation-mandated) technical information on products. Even if that wasn't especially accurate or useful, it existed. For major consumer items that had largely ceased by the 1960s, for personal electronics perhaps the late 1990s / early aughts. Advertising largely relies on sex appeal and image rather than information.

Manufacturer / vendor / service-provider sites are swamped in similar emotional appeals rather than solid information, and it's tedious trying to dig through to any level of technical information. Even then, actual customer-oriented information tends to be relegated to third-party discussion sites, social media, Reddit (still occasionally useful, I very grudgingly admit: <https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49015402>), blogs, videos, and the occasional review site (most of which are also somewhere between highly suspect and useless). May the ghods help you if you want to root or re-ROM a device, and you're directed to highly-sketch English-as-a-fourteenth-language sites.

The highly-rated (NYT Wirecutter) cooker bought a year ago: multiple repairs and three replacements later, it still won't correctly pre-heat to a set point in some baking modes. Satisfactory in most other respects, but as a heavy baker, that somewhat curbs my enthusiasm.

A personal electronics device I'd written of with some happiness on HN has gone no-op, and it's taken me most of a year to even get to the vendor offering an RMA and repair shipping address.

Upgrading household comms (voice, data), and sorting through what options are actually available, all plans, costs, features, and details of service (obligations, total costs, privacy options, etc.) has been a nightmare.

Looking at mobile devices, sorting out how much privacy is possible (my conclusion: phones themselves are inherently surveilled by multiple factors, the only reasonable option is to offload as much activity as possible from them to elsewhere); what device, OS, and software capabilities exist; what various distinctions (chipsets, frequencies, OS variants) imply as to actual capabilities and performance; and elements such as system updates or rootability; require either onerous research or are impossible to find. (One vendor has an otherwise attractive offering that is three years old, I compiled a list of releases dating to 2011 trying to estimate release cadence and possible updates, best I figure there should be a new version in the next six months or so.)

Looking at mobile service, it wasn't until I started asking visitors to run speed tests on their own providers that I realised that 6x greater speeds were available through another network. (Why is there no multi-network test tool widely available, either in software or hardware? That would make a great tool-library lending item.) "Coverage maps" obscure more than they reveal, and site-specific performance is of course highly variable.

Never mind sussing out customer support levels and treatment. Though watching a friend go through a nightmare with ... one of our current vendors ... has strongly coloured my preferences going forward. This would be the same provider with 1/6 the wireless data performance of a competitor....

Information goods (software, services, texts) are inherently complex, and even the best reviews tend to be at best topical. I'm less interested in the unboxing experience than the multi-year retrospective ... after which the original product is almost always discontinued.

Deep information is ... frequently paywalled. You probably would find Consumer Reports worthwhile to subscribe to. Perhaps a few other report sites. Ideally this would be a public service, though with funding sufficiently independent that no one Federal, State, or Local government administration transition could imperil it.

Government regulators in the US, particularly at the national level, increasingly have a trust problem. By all appearances deliberately imposed: <https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49044074>. State agencies lack resources to comprehensively test goods.

Increasingly, products are all but entirely unbranded. Marketing badges are slapped on, only to literally fall off shortly after purchase, if they are present at all. I find tableware, plumbing fixtures, and electronics all entirely bare of a manufacturer's mark. No-name Amazon and Temu brands are the norm. See: <https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49029594>.

It's not just that advertising is intrusive, manipulative, privacy-violating, and annoying, it's fucking useless.

But going out and hunting for information is only very slightly better.

It's a universal market for lemons, and that's not a good sign.

<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Market_for_Lemons>

Somewhat frequently discussed on HN itself (141 hits presently in submissions):

<https://hn.algolia.com/?dateRange=all&page=0&prefix=true&que...>

Outright advertising bans ... might be somewhat premature. Or not. But I'd be quite interested in proposals for extremely punishing tax levels on at least certain classes of goods and services. And am open to bans within given categories: pharmaceuticals, alcohol, tobacco, gambling and gaming, and advertising directed at children, perhaps older adults as well. Also limitations on surveillance, tracking, and direct manipulation methods and practices.

story_title.value: What if we made advertising illegal?

comment_text.value:
I cannot emphasize strongly enough just how deeply pervasive the spam is at Reddit. I'm a mod at the ecommerce subreddit, and I've only caught some of the AI-powered marketing operations because in one particular campaign that was making fictional claims about things I had direct knowledge about. Once I looked into the post history, and started to untangle the web of accounts that formed a self-supporting community of posters and commenters, just subtle enough to get genuine engagement, but specific enough to make the kind of posts that the LLMs will siphon up and regurgitate.

It's not just shady little operations. I'm speaking specifically about the SCAYLE ecommerce platform, in my example. They've got Zalando money to play with, and as a German platform that's trying to break into the North American market, it appears they've made a bet on indirectly spamming the LLMs with fictional tales of commerce replatforming horror stories. At first, they're some of the more interesting topics in a sea of really useless posts, with contributions from people who seem to have some real experience with enterprise ecommerce. I was a little suspicious, but these interaction campaigns were spread out enough that I didn't put the pieces together for months. Of course, to go back on what I said at the top of the paragraph, maybe SCAYLE is shady, and I'm giving them too much credit.

The good news is, some of the AI powered tools that mods have access to are getting better at surfacing suspicious patterns of behavior. However, I still find I have to manually address these campaigns.

In the cat-and-mouse game with these marketing jerks, I'm always reluctant to surface what's working and what isn't. This is an interesting post, but it's going to make things worse. Ah well.

comment_text.value:
I posted this comment in another thread so reposting it here because it seems to be on topic.

---

IMHO, the biggest problem with OpenClaw and other AI agents is that the use-cases are still being discovered. We have deployed several hundred of these to customers and I think this challenge comes from the fact that AI agents are largely perceived as workflow automation tools so when it comes to business process they are seen as a replacement for more established frameworks.

They can automate but they are not reliable. I think of them as work and process augmentation tools but this is not how most customers think in my experience.

However, here are a several legit use-case that we use internally which I can freely discuss.

There is an experimental single-server dev infrastructure we are working on that is slightly flaky. We deployed a lightweight agent in go (single 6MB binary) that connects to our customer-facing API (we have our own agentic platform) where the real agent is sitting and can be reconfigured. The agent monitors the server for various health issues. These could be anything from stalled VMs, unexpected errors etc. It is firecracker VMs that we use in very particular way and we don't know yet the scope of the system. When such situations are detected the agent automatically corrects the problems. It keeps of log what it did in a reusable space (resource type that we have) under a folder called learnings. We use these files to correct the core issues when we have the type to work on the code.

We have an AI agent called Studio Bot. It exists in Slack. It wakes up multiple times during the day. It analyses our current marketing efforts and if it finds something useful, it creates the graphics and posts to be sent out to several of our social media channels. A member of staff reviews these suggestions. Most of the time they need to follow up with subsequent request to change things and finally push the changes to buffer. I also use the agent to generate branded cover images for linkedin, x and reddit articles in various aspect ratios. It is a very useful tool that produces graphics with our brand colours and aesthetics but it is not perfect.

We have a customer support agent that monitors how well we handle support request in zendesk. It does not automatically engage with customers. What it does is to supervise the backlog of support tickets and chase the team when we fall behind, which happens.

We have quite a few more scattered in various places. Some of them are even public.

In my mind, the trick is to think of AI agents as augmentation tools. In other words, instead of asking how can I take myself out of the equation, the better question is how can I improve the situation. Sometimes just providing more contextually relevant information is more than enough. Sometimes, you need a simple helper that own a certain part of the business.

I hope this helps.

story_title.value: OpenClaw isn't fooling me. I remember MS-DOS

It analyses our current marketing efforts and if it finds something useful, it creates the graphics and posts to be sent out to several of our social media channels. A member of staff reviews these suggestions. Most of the time they need to follow up with subsequent request to change things and finally push the changes to buffer. I also use the agent to generate branded cover images for linkedin, x and reddit articles in various aspect ratios. It is a very useful tool that produces graphics with our brand colours and aesthetics but it is not perfect.

We have a customer support agent that monitors how well we handle support request in zendesk. It does not automatically engage with customers. What it does is to supervise the backlog of support tickets and chase the team when we fall behind, which happens.

In my mind, the trick is to think of AI agents as augmentation tools. In other words, instead of asking how can I take myself out of the equation, the better question is how can I improve the situation. Sometimes just providing more contextually relevant information is more than enough. Sometimes, you need a simple helper that own a certain part of the business.

I hope this helps.
